But as the midterms approach, how do activists on the ground see the future of the conservative youth movement? And who, if anyone, can take on Kirk’s mantle? France 24 travelled to the place Turning Point was founded - Phoenix, Arizon

Geopolitics.title: BBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year history
Geopolitics.summary: Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures The BBC is set to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for the first time in the show’s 75-year history, after scrapping plans for a radio drama theatre that was to be the new home of the world’s longest-running soap opera. A pledge to move recordings to the so-called Tea Factory, the BBC’s new Birmingham hub in Digbeth, has become the latest victim of the corporation’s £500m cuts plan . Continue reading...

Geopolitics.title: Former Irish Olympic swimming coach jailed over indecent assaults
Geopolitics.summary: A former Irish Olympic swimming coach has been jailed for indecently assaulting four girls and the attempted rape of one of them.

Geopolitics.title: Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
Geopolitics.summary: Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea Europe live – latest updates Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range. An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling. Continue reading...

Geopolitics.title: More part-time bosses and co-CEOs could keep women in leadership and narrow Australia’s pay gap
Geopolitics.summary: Uneven caring responsibilities combined with a lack of flexible work options have prevented women from staying in senior positions, research suggests Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast More part-time bosses and “co-CEOs” could keep women in leadership and narrow Australia’s gender pay gap, the federal government’s Workplace Gender Equality Agency says. WGEA warned resistance to gender equality was growing and urged employers to make management more flexible to reduce the gender pay gap, where women earn $0.79

Geopolitics.title: 'A lot of Ukrainians are feeling extremely betrayed' by Trump's Russian diesel deal
Geopolitics.summary: Reporting from central Ukraine, FRANCE 24's Gulliver Cragg says that "a lot of Ukrainians are feeling extremely betrayed by a country that until recently they saw not only as an ally but as a beacon of freedom and democracy, a country whose values they should aspire to. All of that is falling apart very quickly and Ukrainians' admiration for the United States is disintegrating."

Geopolitics.title: Seafarer's union official says crews offered big money to transit Strait of Hormuz
Geopolitics.summary: As attacks continue to mount on shipping vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, a seafarer's union official says some crews are being offered big rewards for making the crossing.

Geopolitics.title: Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat over North Korean POWs?
Geopolitics.summary: Seoul and Kyiv are trading accusations after the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea. The South insists the move was to be kept secret as it seeks to avoid antagonizing Pyongyang.

Geopolitics.title: Who are the Ukrainian 'volunteers' under Russian command?
Geopolitics.summary: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.

Geopolitics.title: Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV
Geopolitics.summary: The actor portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator, in his latest film.

Geopolitics.title: Harrowing accounts of violence and sex abuse in women's prison told in new podcast
Geopolitics.summary: Madi Bolanos and Anna Sussman's new podcast We Are Jane Doe, by KQED and Snap Studios, investigates rampant sex abuse at the Central California Women's Facility in Chowchilla, Ca.

Science.title: Economics Nobel awarded for work on stabilizing economies in crisis
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03251-4 Laureates share award that builds on the theories that contributed to governments intervening during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Science.title: Electoral integrity under pressure as elections faced persistent threats in 2025
Science.summary: Elections across the world faced a wide range of pressures on electoral integrity in 2025, from violence and misinformation and disinformation to electoral management malfunctions, cyberattacks and natural hazards, according to a new report.

Science.title: Measuring wildfire plumes to predict extreme fire behavior
Science.summary: Predicting the unpredictable starts with understanding how extreme wildfires develop and under what conditions. This knowledge is essential to better anticipate and respond to them. To achieve this, firefighter and researcher Marc Castellnou and the GRAF/Bombers Catalonia team measure the atmosphere both inside and outside wildfire plumes.

Science.title: Global satellite data reveal widening recovery gap between urban and rural vegetation
Science.summary: A global study has revealed a striking divergence in how urban and rural vegetation respond to climate stress. The study was led by Jin Wu from the School of Biological Sciences, Faculty of Science, and professor Yuyu Zhou from the Department of Geography, Faculty of Social Sciences, at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), with Dr. Zhengfei Guo as the first author.

Science.title: Major cities worldwide are sinking, satellite data reveal
Science.summary: Land subsidence is the gradual sinking of the ground, which can damage buildings, foundations, and drainage and sewage systems, and may increase flood risks. However, information on land subsidence dynamics remains limited, which makes it difficult for policymakers to identify where risks are intensifying and where urgent intervention may be needed. Previous assessments have often used different methods or time periods, or focused only on small numbers of cities, which has made global comparisons difficult.

Science.title: What does a PhD pay? Data reveal huge gaps across Europe
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03181-1 Earnings come in a combination of scholarships and salaries and vary widely between countries, an analysis by international federation Eurodoc reveals.

Science.title: Award-winning microscopy image disqualified over AI use
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03240-7 The incident has prompted discussions about the use of artificial intelligence in scientific imagery.

Science.title: NASA’s SpaceX CRS-35 Mission to Launch Health Research
Science.summary: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration. This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through […]

Science.title: Reinforced vertebrae allow plunge-diving seabirds to survive high-speed impact
Science.summary: A northern gannet scans the sea for fish from 100 feet (30 meters) in the air. Upon seeing a school, it pitches its body into a nosedive, somehow breaking the surface at 70 miles per hour (113 kilometers per hour) without breaking its neck. This daring maneuver seems to defy the laws of nature, but it's standard hunting behavior for plunge-diving seabirds.

Science.title: New research traces the origins and human impact of Britain's largest medieval lead industry through ancient teeth
Science.summary: The first definitive evidence of when post-Roman lead production began in one of Europe's largest medieval lead-producing regions, the Derbyshire Peak District in central England, has been uncovered by archaeologists after centuries of mining had erased much of the archaeological evidence. The work has been published in Antiquity.

Science.title: Vapor-based method creates ultralight aerogels without conventional liquid-based chemistry
Science.summary: Researchers at National Taiwan University (NTU), working across the College of Engineering, College of Medicine and National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH), have developed a new method for producing aerogels, introducing what they describe as the world's first purely gaseous-born aerogel fabrication platform. The study is published in Nature Communications.

Science.title: Hidden signals in sleep can predict future health
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03207-8 From a single night of sleep, AI tools can uncover physiological patterns linked to disease and mortality that are missed by conventional sleep measures.

Science.title: Baby tooth places macaques in northern Germany more than 300,000 years ago
Science.summary: A research team from the Senckenberg Centre for Human Evolution and Palaeoenvironment at the University of Tübingen and Leiden University in the Netherlands has examined a tooth from the Schöningen archaeological site in Lower Saxony. The study was published in Quaternary Environments and Humans.

Science.title: SpaceX launching 6,300 pounds of cargo to the ISS on Oct. 13: Watch it live
Science.summary: SpaceX will launch more than 3 tons of cargo toward the International Space Station on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Science.title: Chemical disorder gives new ceramic film magnetic properties for potential low-power electronics
Science.summary: A material thinner than a human hair may foster faster computing devices that demand less energy and store more data, according to a multi-institutional team led by researchers in the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences.

Science.title: 'Autonomy always begins with something a human hands it': Who's responsible when an AI agent goes rogue?
Science.summary: Hacking incidents by AI agents are creating a legal minefield. The developers and deployers of rogue bots could be held liable.

Science.title: Does the decline of book reading mark the end of rational thinking?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03224-7 Smartphones and artificial intelligence are undermining our ability to follow a complex argument, with grave consequences.

Science.title: Primordial helium further confirms our understanding of the Big Bang
Science.summary: In the early moments of the big bang, two elements were forged: hydrogen and helium. Technically, the tiniest traces of light elements such as lithium were produced as well, but nothing of consequence. The early universe was about three parts hydrogen to one part helium. All the heavier elements, from the oxygen in your lungs to the iron in your blood, were created through astrophysical processes—fused in stars, formed in supernovae or scattered by the collisions of neutron stars. Even in the present cosmos, heavier elements are so cosmically rare that astronomers group them all as metals.

Science.title: Bacterial antiviral defense suggests ancient link to human chromosome protection
Science.summary: A new antiviral defense system discovered by Columbia scientists could be adapted in the future into a gene editor that slows down aging in our cells and improves cancer therapies. At the same time, the discovery also sheds light on an ancient event in evolution that may have helped set the stage for the emergence of higher organisms.

Science.title: Private, offline and yours: how to search the literature with local AI systems
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03227-4 Concerns about privacy, reproducibility and cost are prompting scientists to use models on their computers rather than in the cloud.

Science.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.

Science.title: What 2024's record-breaking rainfall says about the next El Niño
Science.summary: Though strong El Niños have occurred only four times in as many decades, 2024's intense El Niño is already getting a sequel. New UCLA research shows that 2024 broke the record for extreme rainfall, with 40% of that increase tied to global warming—and conditions are ripe for a repeat.

Science.title: Tiny fossils reveal a missing chapter of ocean life after Snowball Earth
Science.summary: A rare assemblage of micro- and macro-fossils found in a roadside outcrop in South China, featuring thin ribbons, branching shapes and a tiny balloon on a stalk, offers a glimpse of marine life after one of Earth's most extreme ice ages.

Science.title: Stabilizing a simple amino acid opens a path to biodegradable sensors
Science.summary: The humble amino acid glycine—the simplest of all amino acids—is everywhere. The human body produces it, and it helps make up our skin, bones and ligaments. It's found in meats like beef and has even been discovered in comets returned from outer space.

Science.title: Fijian bee genomics suggest 99% effective population decline since European colonization
Science.summary: The decline of pollinator species due to habitat loss and pesticide use over recent decades has been a global concern. Pollinators like bees and butterflies support both wild plants and agricultural food production, but many species are threatened and remain poorly studied. It's estimated that bees, in particular, pollinate between 78% and 94% of all plant species.

Science.title: Nanostructure-assisted ultrasound shows potential for Parkinson's treatment
Science.summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the most common neurological disorders associated with later life, and its prevalence rises sharply with age. It affects the brain systems that control movement, often causing tremor, stiffness, slowness and problems with balance, all of which can reduce independence and quality of life in older adults. The condition is mainly linked to the gradual loss of dopamine-producing nerve cells.

Science.title: Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
Science.summary: Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants.

Science.title: Water-based process turns wood industry byproduct into carbon nanofibers for sodium-ion batteries
Science.summary: A new study led by researchers at the University of Limerick (UL) has identified a new battery material from a renewable wood industry byproduct that could help reduce reliance on scarce and expensive materials.

Science.title: Antarctic Sea Ice Grows to Its 2026 Maximum
Science.summary: The ice reached its third-lowest maximum extent since satellite observations began.

Science.title: Scientists discover vanilla’s hidden healing potential
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered that vanillin, the compound that gives vanilla its distinctive flavor, has powerful properties that could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and promote wound healing. The inexpensive, widely available ingredient could one day become an important component of advanced wound treatments and regenerative medicine.

Science.title: NASA demonstrates next-generation heat shield technologies
Science.summary: NASA is taking an unusual approach to testing heat shields that can keep astronauts safe as they return from missions to the moon and Mars: taking out the trash.

Science.title: High-speed video reveals how honey bee stingers keep pumping venom after detachment
Science.summary: Australian scientists have used high-speed video to uncover the unique mechanism that allows a honey bee's stinger to continue to pump venom into its target even after it has separated from the bee's body.

Science.title: The moon could turn astronauts into 'walking, high voltage capacitors' that accidentally zap spacecraft
Science.summary: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.

Science.title: Gravity and quantum information linked through a derivation of Einstein's equations
Science.summary: Recent research shows that gravity and quantum information are deeply connected and that the shape of spacetime can be traced back to the way information is stored in quantum fields.

Science.title: Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep
Science.summary: Getting better sleep might be as simple as moving a little more every day. Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin found that people who exercised more frequently experienced more deep, restorative sleep, which is essential for brain recovery, memory, and emotional well-being. Surprisingly, just 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day was associated with measurable benefits, while even light activities like walking and standing breaks were linked to better sleep and mood.

Science.title: New light-emitting organic materials could enable deep-tissue bioimaging
Science.summary: Researchers at the University of St Andrews have identified the first examples of a new class of advanced organic semiconductor materials that could one day be used as bioimaging agents, opening up new possibilities for deep-tissue imaging. The study, published in Nature Communications, was led by the Zysman-Colman group in the School of Chemistry at the University of St Andrews in collaboration with the Pal group at Durham University.

Science.title: From nonmagnetic to magnetic: A 2D semiconductor with electrically tunable magnetism
Science.summary: Researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS), in collaboration with scientists from institutions in Switzerland, the Czech Republic and Germany, have demonstrated a way to introduce magnetism into an otherwise nonmagnetic two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor and subsequently control its magnetic properties using an electrical voltage. The findings, published in Science Advances, establish a new platform for investigating electrically controllable magnetism in atomically thin materials, with potential implications for future spintronic technologies.

Science.title: Escape rooms give health care students a safe place to get things wrong
Science.summary: The buzzer goes off. Three occupational therapy students are convinced they have worked out what should happen to their patient next. They are wrong.

Science.title: Elephants continue to shape the savanna even after death
Science.summary: Elephants shape the African savanna. They consume huge amounts of forage, dig for water, topple trees and affect all the animals around them. So, what happens to their outsized presence after these iconic animals pass away?

Science.title: Astronomers witness supermassive black hole gorge on a cosmic meal before 'burping' radio jets 300 days later
Science.summary: Using the NASA spacecraft Swift, astronomers observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal.

Science.title: UAE unveils lander for bold 7-asteroid mission set to launch in 2028 (photos)
Science.summary: In March 2028, the UAE is set to launch an ambitious mission to the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter that will culminate with a landing attempt on a mysteriously reddish space rock.

Science.title: Beyond the solvent fog: watching molecules dance in the crowd
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02970-y A technique called time-resolved X-ray liquidography has been used to shed precision light on the steps involved in a classic chemical reaction.

Science.title: Magnetic sculpting transforms single-source fields into predetermined shapes with mathematical precision
Science.summary: Magnetic fields are invisible yet essential components in technologies ranging from MRI scanners and particle accelerators to atomic clocks and future quantum computers. Each of these applications requires magnetic fields with specific shapes and properties. Today, creating such tailored magnetic fields requires researchers and engineers to design specialized, carefully optimized magnets or large systems of coils for each individual application—a complex and resource-intensive process.

Science.title: Data-driven cricket ratings could reveal undervalued batters and bowlers through peer comparisons
Science.summary: An analytical method could help high-level cricket franchises make more informed decisions about player recruitment, retention and team selection, according to research published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management. The approach uses data envelopment analysis (DEA) to compare efficiency using multiple inputs and outputs. In the world of cricket, this means assessing players against their peers rather than relying on individual statistics.

Science.title: Keep medical doctors in academia — without them, health-care research will suffer
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03225-6 Better career support and more funding stability is needed to retain this invaluable group of scientists.

Science.title: Cholesterol-linked drug boosts gene-targeting potency in early findings
Science.summary: Nucleic acid therapeutics, such as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), have emerged as promising platforms for treating a variety of previously hard-to-treat diseases, including neurological diseases.

Science.title: New study finds the staffing structure of an audit office improves outcomes
Science.summary: Audit firms rely on partners to oversee audits and client relationships; managers to supervise teams and projects; and staff to perform much of the day-to-day work. The more audit partners and managers are involved in supervising and reviewing audit engagements, the better the audits tend to be, according to new research from the University at Buffalo School of Management.

Science.title: High-speed microscopy captures sugar-building enzymes forming rigid pairs and flexible assemblies
Science.summary: From a rigid molecular pair to flexible assemblies with moving domains, the enzymes that build sugar chains display strikingly different behaviors.

Science.title: Inuit figurine: A 700-year-old Indigenous carving of a European made a century before Columbus
Science.summary: This Inuit carving was made a century before Columbus set foot in the Americas and likely depicts a Norseman.

Science.title: How the impossible geometry of 'Tomb Raider III''s UFO level was made
Science.summary: Bigger on the inside? Where have we heard that before?

Science.title: 1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds people who died of 'sharp force' injuries, possibly from a Viking raid
Science.summary: A 1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds the remains of a father, son and four others, a group that may have been victims of Viking raid.

Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11250-8 Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria

Science.title: 'It could have been a very different history': Researchers are finally starting to pin down how many Indigenous people were living in the Americas when Columbus arrived
Science.summary: Archaeologists and geographers have been trying to estimate the pre-1492 population of the Americas for decades. But it's difficult.

Science.title: The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments
Science.summary: Mathematics may hold unexpected clues to understanding Alzheimer’s disease. Scientists have developed a model showing how common metals like copper and zinc may influence the buildup of proteins associated with the disease, while also exploring possible ways to stop the process. The findings could help researchers identify promising strategies for preventing harmful plaque formation.

Science.title: I told ChatGPT to ‘continue’ — it went too far
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02714-y An ambiguous instruction caused the chatbot to send three e-mails from Ying Zhao’s connected account. The incident advanced Zhao’s project, but showed that chatbots need limits.

Science.title: What caused a mysterious atmospheric explosion in Siberia in 1908?
Science.summary: Fire erupted in the morning skies over Siberia on June 30, 1908, as an atmospheric explosion occurred that remains unmatched by any similar event in modern history.
